title: Τρεῖς ἑνὸς ἀντί
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Idomeneus, though half-grey, drives the Trojans to flight, and the poet gives the reason: he has just killed Othryoneus, a newcomer who had promised to drive the Achaeans out of Troy in return for Cassandra. Idomeneus mocks the dead man with a pretended offer of a bride of his own and drags the body off. Asius comes up on foot to defend it, and Idomeneus kills him; Antilochus kills Asius’ charioteer and takes his horses. Deiphobus casts at Idomeneus and misses, but kills Hypsenor, and boasts that Asius is avenged; Antilochus covers his fallen companion while two men carry him off. Idomeneus next kills Alcathous, a man of rank whom Poseidon has enchanted so that he cannot move, and then taunts Deiphobus: three Trojans for one, and he himself is of Zeus’ line.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα μεσαιπόλιός περ ἐὼν Δαναοῖσι κελεύσας
Ἰδομενεὺς Τρώεσσι μετάλμενος ἐν φόβον ὦρσε.
sentences.tr:
entha mesaipolios per eōn Danaoisi keleusas
Idomeneus Trōessi metalmenos en phobon ōrse.
sentences.l:
There, half-grey though he was, having bidden the Danaans,
Idomeneus, springing among the Trojans, roused flight in them.
sentences.i: There Idomeneus, half-grey though he was, called his orders to the Danaans, sprang among the Trojans, and roused them to flight.
sentences.n: Idomeneus, the Cretan leader, is the subject, and the lines that follow say why the Trojans break: he has just killed Othryoneus. ἔνθα ‘there, at that point’. μεσαιπόλιός περ ἐὼν ‘though being half-grey’: περ marks the contrast between his age and what he does, and ἐών is the epic participle of εἰμί (= ὤν). κελεύσας is the aorist participle of κελεύω ‘bid’, with the dative Δαναοῖσι (epic -οισι); μετάλμενος is the aorist participle of μεθάλλομαι ‘spring among’. ἐν … ὦρσε is split (tmesis): ‘roused in them’, and φόβον ‘flight’ is the house word for the fear in battle that makes men run.

sentences.t:
πέφνε γὰρ Ὀθρυονῆα Καβησόθεν ἔνδον ἐόντα,
ὅς ῥα νέον πολέμοιο μετὰ κλέος εἰληλούθει,
sentences.tr:
pephne gar Othryonēa Kabēsothen endon eonta,
hos rha neon polemoio meta kleos eilēlouthei,
sentences.l:
For he killed Othryoneus, from Cabesus, being within,
who had newly come after the report of war,
sentences.i: For he had killed Othryoneus, a man from Cabesus who was then inside the city and had only lately come after the report of war,
sentences.n: The reason for the Trojans’ flight: Idomeneus had killed Othryoneus. γάρ gives the reason; πέφνε is an unaugmented, reduplicated aorist of φένω ‘kill’, and Ὀθρυονῆα the epic accusative of Ὀθρυονεύς. Καβησόθεν ‘from Cabesus’ (-θεν ‘from’) is a place-name. ἔνδον ἐόντα ‘being within’: the Greek does not say within what, and the English takes it to be the city, because the next lines have him promise to drive the Achaeans ‘out of Troy’. ὅς ῥα … εἰληλούθει ‘who had come’ (pluperfect); νέον ‘newly’; μετὰ κλέος ‘after the report’ (κλέος is what is heard, and can also mean ‘fame’).

sentences.t:
ᾔτεε δὲ Πριάμοιο θυγατρῶν εἶδος ἀρίστην
Κασσάνδρην ἀνάεδνον, ὑπέσχετο δὲ μέγα ἔργον,
ἐκ Τροίης ἀέκοντας ἀπωσέμεν υἷας Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.tr:
ēitee de Priamoio thygatrōn eidos aristēn
Kassandrēn anaednon, hypescheto de mega ergon,
ek Troiēs aekontas apōsemen huias Achaiōn.
sentences.l:
and he was asking for the best in form of Priam’s daughters,
Cassandra, without bridal gifts, and he promised a great work,
from Troy, unwilling, to drive away the sons of the Achaeans.
sentences.i: and had asked for Cassandra, the best in form of Priam’s daughters, without bridal gifts, and had promised a great piece of work: to drive the sons of the Achaeans out of Troy against their will.
sentences.n: What Othryoneus wanted, and what he promised in return. ᾔτεε is the imperfect of αἰτέω ‘ask for’ in its uncontracted epic form. Πριάμοιο θυγατρῶν ‘of Priam’s daughters’ (epic genitives -οιο) is a partitive genitive with εἶδος ἀρίστην ‘best in form’, where εἶδος is an accusative of respect: the most beautiful, Cassandra. ἀνάεδνον ‘without bridal gifts’ (ἕδνα): a suitor normally paid the girl’s family, and here he offers a deed instead. ὑπέσχετο ‘promised’. ἀπωσέμεν is the future infinitive of ἀπωθέω ‘push away’ with the epic ending -έμεν (= ἀπώσειν); ἀέκοντας ‘unwilling’ agrees with υἷας (epic accusative of υἱός), so the Achaeans are to be driven off against their will.

sentences.t:
τῷ δ’ ὁ γέρων Πρίαμος ὑπό τ’ ἔσχετο καὶ κατένευσε
δωσέμεναι·
sentences.tr:
tōi d’ ho gerōn Priamos hypo t’ escheto kai kateneuse
dōsemenai·
sentences.l:
And to him the old man Priam both promised and nodded assent
to give her;
sentences.i: Old Priam promised him this and nodded his assent to give her;
sentences.n: Priam’s side of the bargain. τῷ is the article used as a pronoun, ‘to him’ (Othryoneus), and ὁ γέρων ‘the old man’ goes with Πρίαμος. ὑπό τ’ ἔσχετο is one verb split in two (tmesis), ὑπέσχετο ‘promised’, aorist middle of ὑπίσχομαι; τε … καί joins it to κατένευσε ‘nodded assent’ (aorist of κατανεύω). δωσέμεναι is the future infinitive of δίδωμι in the epic ending -έμεναι (= δώσειν), ‘to give’ (her, understood). The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line.

sentences.t: ὃ δὲ μάρναθ’ ὑποσχεσίῃσι πιθήσας.
sentences.tr: ho de marnath’ hyposchesiēisi pithēsas.
sentences.l: and he fought, having trusted in the promises.
sentences.i: and he fought on, trusting in those promises.
sentences.n: What the promises did to him: they kept him fighting. ὃ δέ ‘and he’ is the article as a pronoun, Othryoneus. μάρναθ’ is μάρνατο, imperfect of μάρναμαι ‘fight’, elided. ὑποσχεσίῃσι is the dative plural (epic -ῃσι) of ὑποσχεσίη ‘promise’, and πιθήσας is the aorist participle of πιθέω (= πείθομαι) ‘trust, obey’, which takes the dative. The unit begins mid-line, after the stop.

sentences.t:
Ἰδομενεὺς δ’ αὐτοῖο τιτύσκετο δουρὶ φαεινῷ,
καὶ βάλεν ὕψι βιβάντα τυχών·
sentences.tr:
Idomeneus d’ autoio titysketo douri phaeinōi,
kai balen hypsi bibanta tychōn·
sentences.l:
And Idomeneus aimed at him with his shining spear,
and hit him, stepping high, having hit;
sentences.i: Idomeneus aimed his shining spear at him and hit him squarely as he strode along with a high step;
sentences.n: Idomeneus’ cast finds Othryoneus. αὐτοῖο is the epic genitive (= αὐτοῦ), ‘at him’, after τιτύσκετο, imperfect of τιτύσκομαι ‘aim at’; δουρί is the dative of δόρυ ‘spear’ (the means), and φαεινῷ ‘shining’ is a stock epithet of the spear. βάλεν ‘hit’ is an unaugmented aorist; τυχών ‘having hit’ is the aorist participle of τυγχάνω, ‘having struck the mark’, so the Greek says twice that the spear found him. ὕψι βιβάντα ‘stepping high’: βιβάντα is the accusative participle of βίβημι ‘stride’, and ὕψι ‘on high’ pictures a man walking tall. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line 371.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἤρκεσε θώρηξ
χάλκεος, ὃν φορέεσκε, μέσῃ δ’ ἐν γαστέρι πῆξε.
sentences.tr:
oud’ ērkese thōrēx
chalkeos, hon phoreeske, mesēi d’ en gasteri pēxe.
sentences.l:
nor did the breastplate ward it off,
the bronze one, which he kept carrying, but in the middle belly he fixed it.
sentences.i: Nor did the bronze breastplate that the man wore ward it off, but Idomeneus fixed his spear in the middle of the man’s belly.
sentences.n: The spear goes in, and the armour does not stop it. οὐδ’ ἤρκεσε ‘nor did it ward off’: ἀρκέω has no object here, so ‘it’ (the spear) is supplied; θώρηξ is the breastplate, and ὃν φορέεσκε ‘which he kept carrying’ has the -εσκε ending that marks a habit (here, wearing it regularly). μέσῃ ἐν γαστέρι ‘in the middle belly’, and πῆξε ‘fixed’ is the unaugmented aorist of πήγνυμι. The same words come again at 397–398, said of Antilochus’ kill, and are translated the same.

sentences.t: δούπησεν δὲ πεσών·
sentences.tr: doupēsen de pesōn·
sentences.l: and he fell with a thud;
sentences.i: and he fell with a thud;
sentences.n: Othryoneus is the one who falls. δούπησεν ‘fell with a thud’ is built on δοῦπος ‘thud, heavy sound’ and has no augment (Attic ἐδούπησεν); πεσών ‘having fallen’ is the aorist participle of πίπτω. The same words open line 442, of another man’s fall. The unit is cut at the ano teleia in the middle of the line.

sentences.t: ὃ δ’ ἐπεύξατο φώνησέν τε·
sentences.tr: ho d’ epeuxato phōnēsen te·
sentences.l: and he vaunted and spoke:
sentences.i: and Idomeneus cried out in triumph over him, and spoke:
sentences.n: Idomeneus speaks over the body. ὃ δ’ ‘and he’ is the article as a pronoun, Idomeneus. ἐπεύξατο ‘vaunted, cried out in triumph’ is the aorist of ἐπεύχομαι in its sense of a taunt over a fallen man, not a prayer. φώνησέν τε ‘and spoke’ has the movable -ν. The half-line introduces the speech of 374–382.

sentences.t:
Ὀθρυονεῦ περὶ δή σε βροτῶν αἰνίζομ’ ἁπάντων
εἰ ἐτεὸν δὴ πάντα τελευτήσεις ὅσ’ ὑπέστης
Δαρδανίδῃ Πριάμῳ·
sentences.tr:
Othryoneu peri dē se brotōn ainizom’ hapantōn
ei eteon dē panta teleutēseis hos’ hypestēs
Dardanidēi Priamōi·
sentences.i: “Othryoneus, I commend you above all mortals, if you will truly fulfil everything you undertook to Priam, a descendant of Dardanus;
sentences.n: A mocking speech to a dead man: Idomeneus ‘praises’ him on condition that he keeps a promise he can no longer keep. Ὀθρυονεῦ is the vocative. περὶ … βροτῶν ἁπάντων: περί ‘beyond’ with the genitive of comparison, with σε wedged between; αἰνίζομ’ is αἰνίζομαι ‘I commend, praise’. εἰ ἐτεὸν δή ‘if truly indeed’; τελευτήσεις is the future of τελευτάω ‘fulfil’; ὑπέστης is the aorist of ὑφίσταμαι ‘undertake’ (second person). Δαρδανίδῃ Πριάμῳ is a dative: Priam is called ‘descendant of Dardanus’, a patronymic-type name.

sentences.t: ὃ δ’ ὑπέσχετο θυγατέρα ἥν.
sentences.tr: ho d’ hypescheto thygatera hēn.
sentences.l: and he promised his own daughter.
sentences.i: and he, for his part, promised his own daughter.
sentences.n: The other half of the bargain. ὃ δ’ ‘and he’ is Priam, as against Othryoneus (‘you’) in the previous unit. ὑπέσχετο ‘promised’ is a different verb from ὑπέστης ‘undertook’: the two stand for the two sides of one agreement. ἥν is the possessive ὅς (‘his own’), not the relative: θυγατέρα ἥν ‘his own daughter’, Cassandra. The unit begins mid-line, after the stop. Line 376 is metrically irregular as transmitted: it scans only if the first syllable of θυγατέρα, short by nature, is taken as long in the fifth foot.

sentences.t:
καί κέ τοι ἡμεῖς ταῦτά γ’ ὑποσχόμενοι τελέσαιμεν,
δοῖμεν δ’ Ἀτρεΐδαο θυγατρῶν εἶδος ἀρίστην
Ἄργεος ἐξαγαγόντες ὀπυιέμεν, εἴ κε σὺν ἄμμιν
Ἰλίου ἐκπέρσῃς εὖ ναιόμενον πτολίεθρον.
sentences.tr:
kai ke toi hēmeis tauta g’ hyposchomenoi telesaimen,
doimen d’ Atreïdao thygatrōn eidos aristēn
Argeos exagagontes opuiemen, ei ke syn ammin
Iliou ekpersēis eu naiomenon ptoliethron.
sentences.l:
And we too for you could fulfil these things, having promised them,
and give the best in form of Atreus’-son’s daughters,
having led her out from Argos, to marry, if with us
you sack the well-inhabited citadel of Ilios.
sentences.i: And we, too, could fulfil these promises for you: we would give you the best in form of the daughters of the son of Atreus, bringing her out of Argos for you to marry, if you will sack with us the well-inhabited citadel of Ilios.
sentences.n: Idomeneus turns the taunt into a counter-offer: the Achaeans can promise a bride too. καί κε … τελέσαιμεν is an optative with κε (= ἄν), ‘we too could fulfil’; ὑποσχόμενοι ‘having promised’ is an aorist participle, and τοι is the enclitic dative of σύ, ‘for you’. δοῖμεν is the aorist optative of δίδωμι. Ἀτρεΐδαο ‘of the son of Atreus’ is usually taken as Agamemnon, and εἶδος ἀρίστην ‘best in form’ is as at 365. ἐξαγαγόντες ‘having led out’ has the bride as unstated object; ὀπυιέμεν is the epic infinitive of ὀπυίω ‘take to wife’. ἄμμιν is the Aeolic ἡμῖν; εἴ κε … ἐκπέρσῃς is an aorist subjunctive, ‘if you sack’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἕπε’, ὄφρ’ ἐπὶ νηυσὶ συνώμεθα ποντοπόροισιν
ἀμφὶ γάμῳ, ἐπεὶ οὔ τοι ἐεδνωταὶ κακοί εἰμεν.
sentences.tr:
all’ hepe’, ophr’ epi nēusi synōmetha pontoporoisin
amphi gamōi, epei ou toi eednōtai kakoi eimen.
sentences.l:
But follow me, so that by the sea-crossing ships we may come to terms
about the marriage, since we are not base givers of bridal gifts.”
sentences.i: But follow me, so that we may settle the marriage by the sea-crossing ships, since we are no poor givers of bridal gifts.”
sentences.n: The offer is made concrete: follow me to the ships and we will settle terms. ἕπε’ is ἕπεο, imperative of ἕπομαι ‘follow’. ὄφρα … συνώμεθα is a first-person plural subjunctive of purpose; the form is usually referred to συνίημι ‘bring together’ (middle, ‘come to terms’), and the sense ‘settle’ is fixed by ἀμφὶ γάμῳ ‘about the marriage’. ἐπὶ νηυσὶ ποντοπόροισιν ‘by the sea-crossing ships’. ἐεδνωταί ‘givers of bridal gifts’ is a rare word built on ἕεδνα; κακοί ‘base, poor’. τοι is the particle ‘you may be sure’ (or the dative ‘for you’). The cruelty is that the ‘bridegroom’ is being dragged off dead, as the next unit shows.

sentences.t:
ὣς εἰπὼν ποδὸς ἕλκε κατὰ κρατερὴν ὑσμίνην
ἥρως Ἰδομενεύς·
sentences.tr:
hōs eipōn podos helke kata kraterēn hysminēn
hērōs Idomeneus·
sentences.l:
So having spoken, he was dragging by the foot through the strong battle
the hero Idomeneus;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and the hero Idomeneus dragged him by the foot through the strong battle;
sentences.n: Idomeneus drags Othryoneus’ body away. ὣς εἰπών ‘so having spoken’ (aorist participle of εἶπον). ποδὸς ‘by the foot’ is a genitive of the part taken hold of; ἕλκε is the unaugmented imperfect of ἕλκω ‘drag’; κατά with the accusative ‘through’; κρατερὴν ὑσμίνην ‘the strong battle’. ἥρως ‘the hero’ is a title that stands with the name, and the name is held to the end of the clause. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line 384.

sentences.t:
τῷ δ’ Ἄσιος ἦλθ’ ἐπαμύντωρ
πεζὸς πρόσθ’ ἵππων·
sentences.tr:
tōi d’ Asios ēlth’ epamyntōr
pezos prosth’ hippōn·
sentences.l:
and to him Asius came, a defender,
on foot in front of the horses;
sentences.i: Asius came to the dead man’s defence, on foot in front of his horses;
sentences.n: A defender arrives for the dead man. τῷ is the article as a pronoun, ‘to him’ (Othryoneus). ἦλθ’ is ἦλθε, elided. ἐπαμύντωρ ‘defender’ is built on ἐπαμύνω ‘come to the defence of’. πεζὸς ‘on foot’ and πρόσθ’ ἵππων ‘in front of the horses’ set up the next lines: his chariot follows close behind him.

sentences.t:
τὼ δὲ πνείοντε κατ’ ὤμων
αἰὲν ἔχ’ ἡνίοχος θεράπων·
sentences.tr:
tō de pneionte kat’ ōmōn
aien ech’ hēniochos therapōn·
sentences.l:
and the two, breathing down on his shoulders,
the charioteer, the attendant, was always holding;
sentences.i: while the two horses, breathing down on his shoulders, were always held close by his charioteer, his attendant;
sentences.n: The horses follow so close that they breathe on Asius’ shoulders. τὼ is the dual of the article used as a pronoun, ‘the two’ (his two horses), and it is the object of ἔχ’; πνείοντε is the dual participle of πνέω ‘breathe’; κατ’ ὤμων is κατά with the genitive, ‘down on the shoulders’. ἔχ’ is ἔχε, an unaugmented imperfect of ἔχω ‘was holding’, and its subject ἡνίοχος θεράπων ‘charioteer, attendant’ comes last, so the Greek puts the object first and the subject at the end, and the literal layer keeps that order. The unit begins and ends mid-line.

sentences.t:
ὃ δὲ ἵετο θυμῷ
Ἰδομενῆα βαλεῖν·
sentences.tr:
ho de hieto thymōi
Idomenēa balein·
sentences.l:
and he was eager in spirit
to hit Idomeneus;
sentences.i: and Asius was eager in spirit to hit Idomeneus;
sentences.n: Asius means to strike Idomeneus. ὃ δέ ‘and he’ is Asius, the article as a pronoun. ἵετο is the imperfect middle of ἵεμαι ‘be eager’, with the infinitive βαλεῖν ‘to hit’ (aorist); θυμῷ ‘in spirit’ is a dative of respect. Ἰδομενῆα is the epic accusative of Ἰδομενεύς.

sentences.t:
ὃ δέ μιν φθάμενος βάλε δουρὶ
λαιμὸν ὑπ’ ἀνθερεῶνα, διὰ πρὸ δὲ χαλκὸν ἔλασσεν.
sentences.tr:
ho de min phthamenos bale douri
laimon hyp’ anthereōna, dia pro de chalkon elassen.
sentences.l:
but he, having got in before him, hit him with his spear
in the throat under the chin, and clean through drove the bronze.
sentences.i: but Idomeneus got in first and hit him with his spear in the throat under the chin, driving the bronze clean through.
sentences.n: Watch the pronouns: the second ὃ δέ (‘but he’) is Idomeneus, not Asius, and the Greek marks the change of subject only by the particle and the pronoun. φθάμενος is the aorist participle of φθάνω ‘be first, anticipate’, with μιν ‘him’; βάλε ‘hit’ takes two accusatives, the man and the part, λαιμόν ‘throat’ with ὑπ’ ἀνθερεῶνα ‘up under the chin’. διὰ πρὸ δὲ … ἔλασσεν is split (tmesis): ‘drove right through’, with χαλκόν ‘the bronze’ for the spear-point, and ἔλασσεν the aorist of ἐλαύνω ‘drive’.

sentences.t:
ἤριπε δ’ ὡς ὅτε τις δρῦς ἤριπεν ἢ ἀχερωῒς
ἠὲ πίτυς βλωθρή, τήν τ’ οὔρεσι τέκτονες ἄνδρες
ἐξέταμον πελέκεσσι νεήκεσι νήϊον εἶναι·
sentences.tr:
ēripe d’ hōs hote tis drys ēripen ē acherōïs
ēe pitys blōthrē, tēn t’ ouresi tektones andres
exetamon pelekessi neēkesi nēïon einai·
sentences.i: He fell as an oak falls, or a white poplar, or a tall pine, that builders cut down on the mountains with newly sharpened axes to be ship’s timber;
sentences.n: A tree simile for the fall of a big man. ἤριπε is the aorist of ἐρείπω ‘fall in a heap’, repeated inside the simile (ὡς ὅτε ‘as when’). The trees are δρῦς ‘oak’, ἀχερωΐς (usually taken as the white poplar) and πίτυς ‘pine’, with βλωθρή ‘tall’ (the usual gloss). τήν τ’ ‘which’ has the epic τε of a general statement; οὔρεσι is the dative plural of οὖρος (= ὄρος); τέκτονες ἄνδρες ‘builders’; πελέκεσσι νεήκεσι ‘with newly sharpened axes’ (νεήκης, from νέος ‘new’ and a word for an edge); νήϊον εἶναι ‘to be ship-timber’. The aorists of the simile state what always happens, so English uses the present.

sentences.t:
ὣς ὃ πρόσθ’ ἵππων καὶ δίφρου κεῖτο τανυσθεὶς
βεβρυχὼς κόνιος δεδραγμένος αἱματοέσσης.
sentences.tr:
hōs ho prosth’ hippōn kai diphrou keito tanystheis
bebrychōs konios dedragmenos haimatoessēs.
sentences.l:
so he in front of the horses and the chariot lay stretched out,
roaring, clutching at the bloody dust.
sentences.i: So he lay stretched out in front of his horses and chariot, roaring, clutching at the bloody dust.
sentences.n: ὣς ‘so’ answers the simile: Asius lies as the felled tree lies. κεῖτο ‘lay’ (imperfect of κεῖμαι); τανυσθείς ‘stretched out’ (aorist passive participle of τανύω). βεβρυχώς is the perfect participle of βρύχω ‘roar’; the verb is also used for grinding the teeth, and which is meant here is not certain. δεδραγμένος is the perfect participle of δράσσομαι ‘grasp’, and it takes the genitive κόνιος (the epic genitive of κόνις) ‘of the dust’: he clutches at it. αἱματοέσσης ‘bloody’.

sentences.t:
ἐκ δέ οἱ ἡνίοχος πλήγη φρένας ἃς πάρος εἶχεν,
οὐδ’ ὅ γ’ ἐτόλμησεν δηΐων ὑπὸ χεῖρας ἀλύξας
ἂψ ἵππους στρέψαι, τὸν δ’ Ἀντίλοχος μενεχάρμης
δουρὶ μέσον περόνησε τυχών·
sentences.tr:
ek de hoi hēniochos plēgē phrenas has paros eichen,
oud’ ho g’ etolmēsen dēïōn hypo cheiras alyxas
aps hippous strepsai, ton d’ Antilochos menecharmēs
douri meson peronēse tychōn·
sentences.l:
And his charioteer was struck out of the wits that he had before,
nor did he dare, having escaped from under the enemies’ hands,
back to turn the horses; and him Antilochus, steadfast in the fray,
with his spear in the middle pierced, having hit;
sentences.i: Asius’ charioteer was struck out of the wits he had before, and did not dare, though he had escaped the enemies’ hands, to turn the horses back; and Antilochus, steadfast in the fray, pierced him in the middle with his spear, hitting him;
sentences.n: The charioteer panics and does not turn back, and Antilochus kills him. ἐκ … πλήγη is split (tmesis): ‘was struck out of’, an unaugmented aorist passive of ἐκπλήσσω; φρένας ἃς πάρος εἶχεν ‘the wits which he had before’, and οἱ ‘his’ is Asius’. οὐδ’ ὅ γε ἐτόλμησεν ‘nor did he dare’ has the infinitive στρέψαι ‘to turn’, with ἂψ ‘back’; δηΐων ‘of the enemies’ (δήϊος ‘hostile’, used as a noun); ἀλύξας ‘having escaped’. μενεχάρμης ‘steadfast in the fray’ is Antilochus’ stock epithet. περόνησε is the aorist of περονάω ‘pierce’, μέσον ‘in the middle’, and τυχών ‘having hit’ as at 371. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line 397.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἤρκεσε θώρηξ
χάλκεος ὃν φορέεσκε, μέσῃ δ’ ἐν γαστέρι πῆξεν.
sentences.tr:
oud’ ērkese thōrēx
chalkeos hon phoreeske, mesēi d’ en gasteri pēxen.
sentences.l:
nor did the breastplate ward it off,
the bronze one, which he kept carrying, but in the middle belly he fixed it.
sentences.i: Nor did the bronze breastplate that the man wore ward it off, but Antilochus fixed his spear in the middle of the man’s belly.
sentences.n: The same words as 371–372, now of Antilochus’ kill, and translated the same. Here the breastplate is the charioteer’s, and πῆξεν has the movable -ν that πῆξε lacks at 372. The unit begins mid-line.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὃ ἀσθμαίνων εὐεργέος ἔκπεσε δίφρου,
ἵππους δ’ Ἀντίλοχος μεγαθύμου Νέστορος υἱὸς
ἐξέλασε Τρώων μετ’ ἐϋκνήμιδας Ἀχαιούς.
sentences.tr:
autar ho asthmainōn euergeos ekpese diphrou,
hippous d’ Antilochos megathymou Nestoros huios
exelase Trōōn met’ eÿknēmidas Achaious.
sentences.l:
But he, panting, fell out of the well-made chariot,
and the horses Antilochus, son of great-hearted Nestor,
drove them out from the Trojans among the well-greaved Achaeans.
sentences.i: The charioteer, panting, fell out of the well-made chariot, and Antilochus, son of great-hearted Nestor, drove the horses out from the Trojans among the well-greaved Achaeans.
sentences.n: The charioteer falls dead and Antilochus takes Asius’ horses. αὐτάρ ‘but’; ὃ is the charioteer, the article as a pronoun; ἀσθμαίνων ‘panting’; ἔκπεσε is the unaugmented aorist of ἐκπίπτω; εὐεργέος ‘well-made’. ἵππους ‘horses’ is the object of ἐξέλασε ‘drove out’, which lacks the augment and comes in the last line, a formula for carrying off captured horses. ‘Antilochus, son of great-hearted Nestor’ is a noun–epithet phrase with a patronymic; μεγαθύμου ‘great-hearted’.

sentences.t:
Δηΐφοβος δὲ μάλα σχεδὸν ἤλυθεν Ἰδομενῆος
Ἀσίου ἀχνύμενος, καὶ ἀκόντισε δουρὶ φαεινῷ.
sentences.tr:
Dēïphobos de mala schedon ēlythen Idomenēos
Asiou achnymenos, kai akontise douri phaeinōi.
sentences.l:
And Deiphobus very near came to Idomeneus,
grieving for Asius, and cast with his shining spear.
sentences.i: Deiphobus came very close to Idomeneus, grieving for Asius, and cast his shining spear.
sentences.n: Deiphobus, a Trojan, takes up the fight for Asius. ἤλυθεν is the epic form of ἦλθεν ‘came’; σχεδὸν ‘near’ takes the genitive Ἰδομενῆος (epic -ῆος); μάλα ‘very’. Ἀσίου ἀχνύμενος ‘grieving for Asius’ is a genitive of the cause. ἀκόντισε is the aorist of ἀκοντίζω ‘cast’ (a spear), δουρὶ φαεινῷ ‘with his shining spear’ a dative of means.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὃ μὲν ἄντα ἰδὼν ἠλεύατο χάλκεον ἔγχος
Ἰδομενεύς·
sentences.tr:
all’ ho men anta idōn ēleuato chalkeon enchos
Idomeneus·
sentences.l:
But he, looking straight at it, avoided the bronze spear
Idomeneus;
sentences.i: But Idomeneus, seeing it coming straight at him, avoided the bronze spear;
sentences.n: Idomeneus sees the cast coming and dodges it. ὃ μέν ‘he, for his part’ is the article as a pronoun, set against Deiphobus’ cast; the name Ἰδομενεύς is held to the start of the next line. ἄντα ἰδών ‘looking straight at (it)’; ἠλεύατο ‘avoided’ (aorist of ἀλέομαι), χάλκεον ἔγχος ‘the bronze spear’. The first line is a formula that stands also at 13.184, and is translated as there, with the subject changed. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line 405.

sentences.t:
κρύφθη γὰρ ὑπ’ ἀσπίδι πάντοσ’ ἐΐσῃ,
τὴν ἄρ’ ὅ γε ῥινοῖσι βοῶν καὶ νώροπι χαλκῷ
δινωτὴν φορέεσκε, δύω κανόνεσσ’ ἀραρυῖαν·
sentences.tr:
kryphthē gar hyp’ aspidi pantos’ eïsēi,
tēn ar’ ho ge rhinoisi boōn kai nōropi chalkōi
dinōtēn phoreeske, dyō kanoness’ araruian·
sentences.i: for he was hidden under the shield, equal on every side, that he carried, worked in rounds with ox-hides and flashing bronze, fitted with two bars;
sentences.n: Why the spear missed: the shield. κρύφθη ‘was hidden’ (aorist passive of κρύπτω); πάντοσ’ ἐΐσῃ ‘equal on every side’; τήν is the relative ‘which’, the shield. ῥινοῖσι βοῶν ‘with hides of oxen’; νώροπι χαλκῷ ‘with flashing bronze’ (the meaning of νώροψ is not known, ‘flashing’ is the traditional gloss); δινωτήν ‘worked in rounds’ (‘turned’ or ‘inlaid in rings’; not certain); φορέεσκε has the -εσκε of habit. ἀραρυῖαν ‘fitted’ is a perfect participle of ἀραρίσκω, and δύω κανόνεσσ’ is ‘with two bars’ (κανών ‘rod, bar’): the bars are usually taken as the cross-pieces by which the shield was held. The unit begins mid-line.

sentences.t:
τῇ ὕπο πᾶς ἐάλη, τὸ δ’ ὑπέρπτατο χάλκεον ἔγχος,
καρφαλέον δέ οἱ ἀσπὶς ἐπιθρέξαντος ἄϋσεν
ἔγχεος·
sentences.tr:
tēi hypo pas ealē, to d’ hyperptato chalkeon enchos,
karphaleon de hoi aspis epithrexantos aÿsen
encheos·
sentences.i: he crouched, all of him, beneath it, and the bronze spear flew over, and his shield rang harshly as the spear ran across it;
sentences.n: He crouched under the shield, and the spear sailed over it. τῇ ὕπο is ὑπὸ τῇ ‘beneath which’, with the accent thrown back (the preposition follows its word). πᾶς ἐάλη ‘all of him was pressed in’: ἐάλη is the aorist passive of εἴλω ‘press, hem in’, here ‘crouched’. τὸ δ’ ὑπέρπτατο ‘and it flew over’. καρφαλέον ‘dry’ is an adverb with ἄϋσεν ‘rang’ (the verb of a cry, here of a shield); ἐπιθρέξαντος ἔγχεος is a genitive absolute, ‘the spear having run over it’; οἱ ‘his’. The same dry sound is a man’s cry at 441. The unit ends with the first word of line 410.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἅλιόν ῥα βαρείης χειρὸς ἀφῆκεν,
ἀλλ’ ἔβαλ’ Ἱππασίδην Ὑψήνορα ποιμένα λαῶν
ἧπαρ ὑπὸ πραπίδων, εἶθαρ δ’ ὑπὸ γούνατ’ ἔλυσε.
sentences.tr:
oud’ halion rha bareiēs cheiros aphēken,
all’ ebal’ Hippasidēn Hypsēnora poimena laōn
hēpar hypo prapidōn, eithar d’ hypo gounat’ elyse.
sentences.l:
nor in vain from his heavy hand did he let it go,
but hit Hippasus’-son Hypsenor, shepherd of the people,
in the liver beneath the midriff, and at once he loosed his knees.
sentences.i: Nor did he let it go from his heavy hand in vain, but hit Hypsenor, son of Hippasus, shepherd of the people, in the liver under the midriff, and at once loosed his knees.
sentences.n: Deiphobus’ cast is not wasted: it kills Hypsenor, an Achaean (his companions carry him off at 421–423). The subject is Deiphobus. οὐδ’ ἅλιον ‘nor in vain’: ἅλιος ‘vain’ is a different word from ἅλιος ‘of the sea’; ἀφῆκεν is the aorist of ἀφίημι ‘let go’, with the spear as unstated object, and βαρείης χειρὸς ‘from his heavy hand’ a genitive of separation. Ἱππασίδην ‘son of Hippasus’ is a patronymic; ποιμένα λαῶν ‘shepherd of the people’ a stock phrase. ἧπαρ ὑπὸ πραπίδων ‘in the liver under the midriff’ is a killing blow, and γούνατ’ ἔλυσε ‘loosed his knees’ is the idiom for killing. The unit begins mid-line.

sentences.t: Δηΐφοβος δ’ ἔκπαγλον ἐπεύξατο μακρὸν ἀΰσας·
sentences.tr: Dēïphobos d’ ekpaglon epeuxato makron aÿsas·
sentences.l: And Deiphobus terribly vaunted, shouting loudly:
sentences.i: And Deiphobus cried out terribly in triumph, shouting loudly:
sentences.n: Deiphobus boasts. ἐπεύξατο ‘vaunted’ as at 373; ἔκπαγλον is an adverbial accusative, ‘terribly’ (= ἐκπάγλως); μακρὸν ἀΰσας ‘shouting loudly’, the aorist participle of ἀΰω ‘shout’ with μακρόν as an adverb. The whole line is a speech introduction, and it comes again, with another name, at 445.

sentences.t:
οὐ μὰν αὖτ’ ἄτιτος κεῖτ’ Ἄσιος, ἀλλά ἕ φημι
εἰς Ἄϊδός περ ἰόντα πυλάρταο κρατεροῖο
γηθήσειν κατὰ θυμόν, ἐπεί ῥά οἱ ὤπασα πομπόν.
sentences.tr:
ou man aut’ atitos keit’ Asios, alla he phēmi
eis Aïdos per ionta pylartao krateroio
gēthēsein kata thymon, epei rha hoi ōpasa pompon.
sentences.l:
“Not indeed, in turn, unavenged lies Asius, but him I say,
even going to the (house) of Hades, the gate-fastener, the strong,
will rejoice in his heart, since I gave him an escort.”
sentences.i: “Asius does not lie unavenged; I say that even as he goes to the house of Hades, the strong gate-fastener, he will rejoice in his heart, since I have given him an escort.”
sentences.n: Deiphobus’ boast: Asius has been paid for. ἄτιτος ‘unavenged’ is literally ‘unpaid for’ (ἀ- and τίνω); κεῖτ’ is κεῖται. In ἀλλά ἕ φημι ἕ ‘him’ is the subject of the infinitive γηθήσειν ‘will rejoice’ (future of γηθέω). εἰς Ἄϊδός περ ἰόντα ‘even going to Hades’: the house is understood, and πυλάρταο κρατεροῖο ‘the strong gate-fastener’ stands in apposition (epic genitives -αο, -οιο; what πυλάρτης means is not certain). ἐπεί ῥά οἱ ὤπασα πομπόν ‘since I gave him an escort’: ὤπασα is the aorist of ὀπάζω ‘give as a follower’, and the escort is Hypsenor, whom Deiphobus has just killed and sent down to go with Asius.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφατ’, Ἀργείοισι δ’ ἄχος γένετ’ εὐξαμένοιο,
Ἀντιλόχῳ δὲ μάλιστα δαΐφρονι θυμὸν ὄρινεν·
sentences.tr:
hōs ephat’, Argeioisi d’ achos genet’ euxamenoio,
Antilochōi de malista daïphroni thymon orinen·
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and for the Argives grief arose, as he declared it aloud,
and for Antilochus most of all, wise-minded, it stirred the heart;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and grief came upon the Argives as he declared it aloud, and it stirred most of all the heart of Antilochus, wise-hearted as he was;
sentences.n: The Achaeans’ reaction to the boast. ὣς ἔφατ’ ‘so he spoke’ closes the speech. ἄχος γένετ’ ‘grief arose’ (γένετ’ is the unaugmented aorist of γίγνομαι), Ἀργείοισι ‘for the Argives’; εὐξαμένοιο is a genitive absolute, ‘as he declared (this) aloud’, from the verb that elsewhere may mean ‘pray’ but here is a triumphant claim. Ἀντιλόχῳ … θυμὸν ὄρινεν ‘it stirred Antilochus’ heart’, ὄρινεν the imperfect of ὀρίνω ‘stir’, and μάλιστα ‘most of all’. δαΐφρονι is the stock epithet ‘wise-minded’ (‘wise-hearted’ in the idiomatic English); whether it means ‘wise’ or ‘fierce’ is disputed.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ οὐδ’ ἀχνύμενός περ ἑοῦ ἀμέλησεν ἑταίρου,
ἀλλὰ θέων περίβη καί οἱ σάκος ἀμφεκάλυψε.
sentences.tr:
all’ oud’ achnymenos per heou amelēsen hetairou,
alla theōn peribē kai hoi sakos amphekalypse.
sentences.l:
but not even though grieving did he neglect his own companion,
but running he strode about and for him the shield enfolded.
sentences.i: But grieving though he was, he did not neglect his own companion: he ran up, stood over him, and enfolded him with his shield.
sentences.n: Antilochus defends his companion, the Hypsenor hit at 411. ἀλλ’ οὐδ’ … περ ‘but not even … though’ (ἀχνύμενος ‘grieving’); ἑοῦ is the genitive of the possessive ἑός ‘his own’, and ἀμέλησεν ‘neglected’ takes the genitive ἑταίρου ‘companion’. θέων is the present participle of θέω ‘run’; περίβη is the aorist of περιβαίνω ‘step round’ and stand over a fallen man; σάκος ‘shield’; ἀμφεκάλυψε ‘enfolded’ is the aorist of ἀμφικαλύπτω. The second line is a formula that is used elsewhere of another man, and is translated the same.

sentences.t:
τὸν μὲν ἔπειθ’ ὑποδύντε δύω ἐρίηρες ἑταῖροι
Μηκιστεὺς Ἐχίοιο πάϊς καὶ δῖος Ἀλάστωρ,
νῆας ἔπι γλαφυρὰς φερέτην βαρέα στενάχοντα.
sentences.tr:
ton men epeith’ hypodynte dyō eriēres hetairoi
Mēkisteus Echioio païs kai dios Alastōr,
nēas epi glaphyras pheretēn barea stenachonta.
sentences.l:
Him then, getting under him, two trusty companions,
Mecisteus, Echius’ son, and heavenly Alastor,
to the hollow ships were bearing, heavily groaning.
sentences.i: Then two trusty companions, Mecisteus, son of Echius, and heavenly Alastor, got under him and carried him, groaning heavily, to the hollow ships.
sentences.n: Two other men take the wounded Hypsenor to safety. τὸν ‘him’ is the wounded man, and it is he who is groaning, as the accusative βαρέα στενάχοντα shows. ὑποδύντε is the dual aorist participle of ὑποδύομαι, ‘getting under’ him to take his weight, and φερέτην the dual imperfect of φέρω, ‘were bearing’. δύω ‘two’; ἐρίηρες ‘trusty’ is a stock epithet whose sense is not fully known; πάϊς ‘son’; δῖος ‘heavenly’. νῆας ἔπι γλαφυράς ‘to the hollow ships’: ἔπι follows its noun and so is accented on the first syllable. These lines recur word for word elsewhere in the poem and carry the same English there.

sentences.t:
Ἰδομενεὺς δ’ οὐ λῆγε μένος μέγα, ἵετο δ’ αἰεὶ
ἠέ τινα Τρώων ἐρεβεννῇ νυκτὶ καλύψαι
ἢ αὐτὸς δουπῆσαι ἀμύνων λοιγὸν Ἀχαιοῖς.
sentences.tr:
Idomeneus d’ ou lēge menos mega, hieto d’ aiei
ēe tina Trōōn erebennēi nykti kalypsai
ē autos doupēsai amynōn loigon Achaiois.
sentences.l:
And Idomeneus did not abate his great might, and he was always eager
either some one of the Trojans with murky night to cover,
or himself to fall with a thud, warding off ruin from the Achaeans.
sentences.i: Idomeneus did not let his great might abate; he was always eager either to cover one of the Trojans with murky night, or to fall himself with a thud while warding off ruin from the Achaeans.
sentences.n: Idomeneus presses on, with only two outcomes in view: to kill, or to die defending the Achaeans. οὐ λῆγε is the imperfect of λήγω ‘cease, let up’, here with the accusative μένος μέγα ‘his great might’ as its object, so ‘did not abate’. ἵετο ‘was eager’ (as at 386) is followed by two infinitives, ἠέ … καλύψαι ‘either to cover’ and ἢ … δουπῆσαι ‘or to fall with a thud’ (from δοῦπος ‘thud’, as at 373). To ‘cover with murky night’ is to kill, and ἐρεβεννῇ νυκτί is a dative of means. αὐτός ‘himself’; ἀμύνων λοιγὸν Ἀχαιοῖς ‘warding off ruin from the Achaeans’.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ Αἰσυήταο διοτρεφέος φίλον υἱὸν
ἥρω’ Ἀλκάθοον, γαμβρὸς δ’ ἦν Ἀγχίσαο,
sentences.tr:
enth’ Aisyētao diotrepheos philon huion
hērō’ Alkathoon, gambros d’ ēn Anchisao,
sentences.l:
There of Zeus-nurtured Aesyetes the dear son,
the hero Alcathous, and he was son-in-law of Anchises,
sentences.i: There was the hero Alcathous, the dear son of Zeus-nurtured Aesyetes and son-in-law of Anchises,
sentences.n: A new victim, introduced by his family before we learn what happens to him: Ἀλκάθοον is the object of ἐδάμασσε at 434, and the sentence is held open through a long account of his marriage (429–433) until τὸν τόθ’ picks him up again. ἔνθ’ ‘there, then’. Αἰσυήταο is the epic genitive of Αἰσυήτης; διοτρεφέος ‘Zeus-nurtured’ is a stock epithet of princes; φίλον υἱόν ‘dear son’; ἥρω’ is ἥρωα, ‘hero’. γαμβρός is a son-in-law, here of Anchises, as the next line shows. Line 428 is metrically irregular as transmitted: its fifth foot is a spondee, and in the last foot the short -σα- of Ἀγχίσαο has to count as long.

sentences.t:
πρεσβυτάτην δ’ ὤπυιε θυγατρῶν Ἱπποδάμειαν
τὴν περὶ κῆρι φίλησε πατὴρ καὶ πότνια μήτηρ
ἐν μεγάρῳ·
sentences.tr:
presbytatēn d’ ōpuie thygatrōn Hippodameian
tēn peri kēri philēse patēr kai potnia mētēr
en megarōi·
sentences.i: He had married Hippodameia, the eldest of Anchises’ daughters, whom her father and her lady mother loved deeply at heart in their hall;
sentences.n: His wife, and how she was loved. πρεσβυτάτην ‘eldest’ (superlative) with the partitive θυγατρῶν ‘of the daughters’, those of Anchises; ὤπυιε is the imperfect of ὀπυίω ‘take to wife’, ‘he had married’. τήν is the relative ‘whom’; περὶ κῆρι φίλησε: περί is an adverb ‘exceedingly’, κῆρι the dative of κῆρ ‘heart’, and φίλησε an unaugmented aorist of φιλέω ‘love’. πότνια μήτηρ ‘lady mother’ is a stock phrase; ἐν μεγάρῳ ‘in the hall’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line 431.

sentences.t:
πᾶσαν γὰρ ὁμηλικίην ἐκέκαστο
κάλλεϊ καὶ ἔργοισιν ἰδὲ φρεσί·
sentences.tr:
pasan gar homēlikiēn ekekasto
kalleï kai ergoisin ide phresi·
sentences.l:
for she surpassed the whole company of her age
in beauty and in works and in wits;
sentences.i: for she surpassed the whole company of her own age in beauty, in handiwork, and in wits;
sentences.n: Why she was loved. γάρ gives the reason. ἐκέκαστο is the pluperfect of καίνυμαι ‘excel, surpass’ and takes the accusative ὁμηλικίην, the company of people of her own age. κάλλεϊ is the epic dative of κάλλος ‘beauty’; ἔργοισιν ‘in works’ means what she made with her hands (the Greek says only ‘works’); φρεσί ‘in wits’; ἰδέ ‘and’ (= ἠδέ). The unit begins and ends mid-line.

sentences.t:
τοὔνεκα καί μιν
γῆμεν ἀνὴρ ὤριστος ἐνὶ Τροίῃ εὐρείῃ·
sentences.tr:
touneka kai min
gēmen anēr ōristos eni Troiēi eureiēi·
sentences.l:
for that reason also her
married the man best in broad Troy;
sentences.i: and that is why the best man in broad Troy married her;
sentences.n: Why Alcathous married her: she was the best, and he was the best man. τοὔνεκα is τοῦ ἕνεκα, ‘for that reason’; μιν ‘her’; γῆμεν is γῆμε, the unaugmented aorist of γαμέω ‘marry’, with movable -ν, and its subject is ἀνὴρ ὤριστος, where ὤριστος is ὁ ἄριστος (crasis), ‘the best man’: Alcathous himself, who is taken up by τὸν in the next line. ἐνὶ Τροίῃ εὐρείῃ ‘in broad Troy’ (ἐνί = ἐν). The unit begins mid-line.

sentences.t:
τὸν τόθ’ ὑπ’ Ἰδομενῆϊ Ποσειδάων ἐδάμασσε
θέλξας ὄσσε φαεινά, πέδησε δὲ φαίδιμα γυῖα·
sentences.tr:
ton toth’ hyp’ Idomenēï Poseidaōn edamasse
thelxas osse phaeina, pedēse de phaidima guia·
sentences.l:
Him then, under Idomeneus, Poseidon subdued,
having enchanted his shining eyes, and fettered his glorious limbs;
sentences.i: Poseidon overcame him then beneath Idomeneus, enchanting his shining eyes and fettering his glorious limbs;
sentences.n: Poseidon is helping the Achaeans here, and the god’s spell is what makes Alcathous helpless. τὸν τόθ’ ‘him then’ takes up Alcathous from 427. ὑπ’ Ἰδομενῆϊ ‘beneath Idomeneus’ puts him under Idomeneus’ power; ἐδάμασσε ‘subdued’ is the house rendering of δαμάζω. θέλξας is the aorist participle of θέλγω ‘enchant’; ὄσσε ‘eyes’ is a dual noun with φαεινά ‘shining’; πέδησε is the unaugmented aorist of πεδάω ‘fetter’; φαίδιμα γυῖα ‘glorious limbs’. The next unit says what the spell does.

sentences.t:
οὔτε γὰρ ἐξοπίσω φυγέειν δύνατ’ οὔτ’ ἀλέασθαι,
ἀλλ’ ὥς τε στήλην ἢ δένδρεον ὑψιπέτηλον
ἀτρέμας ἑσταότα στῆθος μέσον οὔτασε δουρὶ
ἥρως Ἰδομενεύς,
sentences.tr:
oute gar exopisō phygeein dynat’ out’ aleasthai,
all’ hōs te stēlēn ē dendreon hypsipetēlon
atremas hestaota stēthos meson outase douri
hērōs Idomeneus,
sentences.l:
for neither to the rear to flee could he nor to avoid it,
but like a pillar or a high-leaved tree
standing motionless, him in the middle of the chest wounded with a spear
the hero Idomeneus,
sentences.i: for he could neither flee to the rear nor avoid the blow; but as he stood motionless like a pillar or a high-leaved tree, the hero Idomeneus stabbed him with his spear in the middle of the chest,
sentences.n: The enchanted man stands rooted, and Idomeneus stabs him. οὔτε … οὔτε ‘neither … nor’; ἐξοπίσω ‘to the rear’; φυγέειν is the uncontracted infinitive of φεύγω; ἀλέασθαι ‘to avoid’ is from ἀλέομαι. ἀλλά brings the comparison: ὥς τε ‘like’, στήλην ‘pillar’, ὑψιπέτηλον ‘high-leaved’ (ὕψι ‘high’, πέταλον ‘leaf’). ἑσταότα ‘standing’, the accusative of the perfect participle of ἵστημι, agrees with the unstated object of οὔτασε (aorist of οὐτάω ‘wound by a thrust’); στῆθος μέσον ‘the middle of the chest’ is the accusative of the part struck, and the subject comes last. The unit is cut at the comma because the sentence runs five lines.

sentences.t:
ῥῆξεν δέ οἱ ἀμφὶ χιτῶνα
χάλκεον, ὅς οἱ πρόσθεν ἀπὸ χροὸς ἤρκει ὄλεθρον·
sentences.tr:
rhēxen de hoi amphi chitōna
chalkeon, hos hoi prosthen apo chroos ērkei olethron·
sentences.l:
and he burst for him around the tunic
bronze, which for him before from his skin warded off destruction;
sentences.i: and burst the bronze tunic about him, which until then had warded destruction off his skin;
sentences.n: The armour that had saved him fails. ῥῆξεν is the aorist of ῥήγνυμι ‘burst’; οἱ ‘for him’; ἀμφί ‘about’; χιτῶνα χάλκεον ‘the bronze tunic’, the body-armour. ὅς οἱ … ἤρκει: ὅς is the relative ‘which’ (not the possessive), οἱ ‘for him’, πρόσθεν ‘before, until then’, ἀπὸ χροὸς ‘from his skin’, and ἤρκει is the imperfect of ἀρκέω ‘ward off’, with ὄλεθρον ‘destruction’ as its object (compare 371, where ἀρκέω has none). The unit begins mid-line.

sentences.t: δὴ τότε γ’ αὖον ἄϋσεν ἐρεικόμενος περὶ δουρί.
sentences.tr: dē tote g’ auon aÿsen ereikomenos peri douri.
sentences.l: then indeed dry he cried out, being torn about the spear.
sentences.i: then at last he cried out harshly, torn about the spear.
sentences.n: The dying man’s cry. δὴ τότε γε ‘then indeed’; αὖον ‘dry’ is an adverb, and the sound is the same harsh, dry sound as the shield’s at 409 (καρφαλέον); ἄϋσεν ‘cried out’. ἐρεικόμενος is the passive participle of ἐρείκω ‘tear’, and περὶ δουρί ‘about the spear’ shows him wrenched on the spear that is fixed in his chest (442).

sentences.t:
δούπησεν δὲ πεσών, δόρυ δ’ ἐν κραδίῃ ἐπεπήγει,
ἥ ῥά οἱ ἀσπαίρουσα καὶ οὐρίαχον πελέμιζεν
ἔγχεος·
sentences.tr:
doupēsen de pesōn, dory d’ en kradiēi epepēgei,
hē rha hoi aspairousa kai ouriachon pelemizen
encheos·
sentences.i: He fell with a thud, the spear fixed in his heart; and the heart, gasping, shook even the butt-end of the spear;
sentences.n: The heart is still beating against the spear. δούπησεν δὲ πεσών is the same phrase as at 373; δόρυ … ἐπεπήγει ‘the spear was fixed’ is a pluperfect of πήγνυμι used as a state. ἥ is the relative ‘which’, and it is the heart: οἱ ‘for him’, ἀσπαίρουσα ‘gasping’ (here a heart’s last convulsions), καί ‘even’, οὐρίαχον ‘butt-end’, the far end of the shaft, which quivers; ἔγχεος ‘of the spear’ depends on οὐρίαχον and is held to the first word of line 444, where the unit ends. πελέμιζεν ‘shook’ is the imperfect of πελεμίζω.

sentences.t: ἔνθα δ’ ἔπειτ’ ἀφίει μένος ὄβριμος Ἄρης·
sentences.tr: entha d’ epeit’ aphiei menos obrimos Arēs·
sentences.l: and there then was letting go the might mighty Ares;
sentences.i: and then mighty Ares let the might go;
sentences.n: The quivering stops. ἔνθα … ἔπειτ’ ‘there, then’; ἀφίει ‘was letting go’ is the imperfect of ἀφίημι; ὄβριμος Ἄρης ‘mighty Ares’ is the war-god himself. Whose might he lets go is not said: it may be the spear’s, which ceases to quiver, or the dying man’s strength. The unit begins mid-line, after the stop.

sentences.t: Ἰδομενεὺς δ’ ἔκπαγλον ἐπεύξατο μακρὸν ἀΰσας·
sentences.tr: Idomeneus d’ ekpaglon epeuxato makron aÿsas·
sentences.l: And Idomeneus terribly vaunted, shouting loudly:
sentences.i: And Idomeneus cried out terribly in triumph, shouting loudly:
sentences.n: Idomeneus answers the boast, with the same introduction as Deiphobus’ at 413: ἐπεύξατο ‘vaunted’, ἔκπαγλον ‘terribly’, μακρὸν ἀΰσας ‘shouting loudly’. He addresses Deiphobus, named in the first word of the speech.

sentences.t:
Δηΐφοβ’ ἦ ἄρα δή τι ἐΐσκομεν ἄξιον εἶναι
τρεῖς ἑνὸς ἀντὶ πεφάσθαι;
sentences.tr:
Dēïphob’ ē ara dē ti eïskomen axion einai
treis henos anti pephasthai;
sentences.l:
“Deiphobus, is it so, then, that we deem it worth something,
three to have been slain in return for one?
sentences.i: “Deiphobus, is it so, then, that we reckon it worth anything, three slain in return for one?
sentences.n: Idomeneus turns Deiphobus’ own reckoning against him: three Trojans (Othryoneus, Asius, Alcathous) have fallen for the one Achaean he has killed. Δηΐφοβ’ is the vocative, elided. ἦ ἄρα δή opens a question. ἐΐσκομεν is the present of ἐΐσκω, here ‘deem, reckon’ (not its other sense ‘liken’); whether ‘we’ is Idomeneus alone or he and Deiphobus is not said. τι ἄξιον εἶναι ‘to be worth something’; τρεῖς ἑνὸς ἀντὶ πεφάσθαι ‘three to have been slain in return for one’, where πεφάσθαι is the perfect passive infinitive of the verb of killing (compare πέφνε at 363). The question ends at the question mark in mid-line 447.

sentences.t: ἐπεὶ σύ περ εὔχεαι οὕτω.
sentences.tr: epei sy per eucheai houtō.
sentences.l: since you yourself declare so.
sentences.i: since you yourself declare it so.
sentences.n: The reason for the sarcasm: Deiphobus has made this kind of reckoning himself. ἐπεί ‘since’; σύ περ ‘you yourself’; εὔχεαι is the epic uncontracted second person of εὔχομαι, here ‘declare’ in the sense of boast, as at 417; οὕτω ‘so’ points back to Deiphobus’ own boast at 414–416. The unit begins mid-line, after the question mark.

sentences.t:
δαιμόνι’ ἀλλὰ καὶ αὐτὸς ἐναντίον ἵστασ’ ἐμεῖο,
ὄφρα ἴδῃ οἷος Ζηνὸς γόνος ἐνθάδ’ ἱκάνω,
ὃς πρῶτον Μίνωα τέκε Κρήτῃ ἐπίουρον·
sentences.tr:
daimoni’ alla kai autos enantion histas’ emeio,
ophra idēi hoios Zēnos gonos enthad’ hikanō,
hos prōton Minōa teke Krētēi epiouron·
sentences.i: Strange man, stand and face me yourself, so that you may see what sort of offspring of Zeus I am, come here, he who first begot Minos to be guardian of Crete;
sentences.n: Idomeneus names his descent. δαιμόνι’ is the vocative of δαιμόνιος, ‘strange man’, a word for someone whose conduct puzzles the speaker; reproach or pity is uncertain. ἀλλὰ καὶ αὐτός ‘but you yourself too’; ἵστασ’ is ἵστασο, present imperative middle of ἵστημι ‘stand’. ὄφρα ἴδῃ ‘so that you may see’: the person is second, since Deiphobus is addressed; the ending is explained either as a middle ἴδῃ(αι) or as an active with its -ς lost. Ζηνὸς γόνος ‘offspring of Zeus’. ὅς in the last line is Zeus: τέκε is the unaugmented aorist ‘begot’, and Κρήτῃ ἐπίουρον ‘guardian for Crete’ is the predicate with Μίνωα.

sentences.t:
Μίνως δ’ αὖ τέκεθ’ υἱὸν ἀμύμονα Δευκαλίωνα,
Δευκαλίων δ’ ἐμὲ τίκτε πολέσσ’ ἄνδρεσσιν ἄνακτα
Κρήτῃ ἐν εὐρείῃ·
sentences.tr:
Minōs d’ au teketh’ huion amymona Deukaliōna,
Deukaliōn d’ eme tikte poless’ andressin anakta
Krētēi en eureiēi·
sentences.i: and Minos in turn begot a blameless son, Deucalion, and Deucalion begot me to be lord over many men in broad Crete;
sentences.n: The descent in full: Zeus, Minos, Deucalion, Idomeneus, so that Idomeneus is Zeus’ great-grandson. Μίνως δ’ αὖ ‘and Minos in turn’; τέκεθ’ is τέκετο, aorist middle of τίκτω ‘begot’ (of a father); ἀμύμονα ‘blameless’ is a stock epithet whose real sense is not known. τίκτε is an unaugmented imperfect of τίκτω; πολέσσ’ ἄνδρεσσιν ‘for many men’ (dative plural, epic -εσσι) with ἄνακτα ‘lord’. Κρήτῃ ἐν εὐρείῃ ‘in broad Crete’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line 453.

sentences.t:
νῦν δ’ ἐνθάδε νῆες ἔνεικαν
σοί τε κακὸν καὶ πατρὶ καὶ ἄλλοισι Τρώεσσιν.
sentences.tr:
nyn d’ enthade nēes eneikan
soi te kakon kai patri kai alloisi Trōessin.
sentences.l:
and now hither the ships brought,
to you an evil and to your father and to the other Trojans.”
sentences.i: But now the ships have brought me here, an evil to you, to your father, and to the other Trojans.”
sentences.n: The point of the genealogy: Idomeneus has come as a curse on Deiphobus’ side. νῦν δ’ ‘but now’; ἐνθάδε ‘here’; νῆες ἔνεικαν ‘the ships brought’, with ἔνεικαν an aorist without augment and the object ‘me’ left unsaid. σοί τε κακὸν καὶ πατρὶ καὶ ἄλλοισι Τρώεσσιν: κακόν ‘an evil’ stands in apposition to the persons, ‘as an evil for you, for your father (Deiphobus’ father, Priam), and for the other Trojans’ (dative plural, epic -εσσιν). The speech ends here. The unit begins mid-line.
